title: Foolishness to this age
source_text: Ἐπεὶ δ᾿ ὁ Κέλσος ἔθηκεν ὡς λεγόμενον ὑπὸ πολλῶν Χριστιανῶν „κακὸν μέν γε ἡ ἐν τῷ βίῳ σοφία ἀγαθὸν δ᾿ ἡ μωρία“. λεκτέον ὅτι συκοφαντεῖ τὸν λόγον. μὴ ἐκθέμενος αὐτὴν τὴν παρὰ τῷ Παύλῳ κειμένην λέξιν οὕτως ἔχουσαν· „εἴ τις δοκεῖ σοφὸς εἶναι ἐν ὑμῖν, ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ μωρὸς γενέσθω. ἵνα γένηται σοφός· ἡ γὰρ σοφία τοῦ κόσμου τούτου μωρία παρὰ θεῷ ἐστιν.“ οὐκοῦν ὁ μὲν ἀπόστολός φησιν οὐχ ἁπλῶς· „ἡ σοφία μωρία παρὰ θεῷ ἐστιν.“ ἀλλ᾿ „ἡ σοφία τοῦ κόσμου τούτου.“ καὶ πάλιν οὐκ „εἴ τις δοκεῖ σοφὸς εἶναι ἐν ὑμῖν“ ἁπαξαπλῶς „μωρὸς γενέσθω,“ ἀλλ᾿ „ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ μωρὸς γενέσθω, ἵνα γένηται σοφός.“ „σοφίαν“ οὖν „τούτου τοῦ αἰῶνος“ λέγομεν τὴν κατὰ τὰς γραφὰς καταργουμένην πᾶσαν ψευδοδοξοῦσαν φιλοσοφίαν· καὶ μωρίαν λέγομεν ἀγαθὸν οὐκ ἀπολελυμένως, ἀλλ᾿ ὅτε τις τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ γίνεται „μωρός“· ὡς εἰ λέγοιμεν καὶ τὸν Πλατωνικὸν, πιστεύοντα τῇ ἀθανασίᾳ τῆς ψυχῆς καὶ τοῖς περὶ αὐτῆς λεγομένοις περὶ μετενσωματώσεως, μωρίαν ἀνειληφέναι ὡς πρὸς τοὺς Στωϊκοὺς διασύροντας τὴν τούτων συγκατάθεσιν, καὶ ὡς πρὸς Περιπατητικοὺς θρυλοῦντας τὰ Πλάτωνος „τερετίσματα,“ καὶ ὡς πρὸς Ἐπικουρείους δεισιδαιμονίαν ἐγκαλοῦντας τοῖς εἰσάγουσι πρόνοιαν καὶ θεὸν ἐφιστᾶσι τοῖς ὅλοις. ἔτι δὲ ὅτι καὶ κατὰ τὸ τῷ λόγῳ ἀρέσκον πολλῷ διαφέρει μετὰ λόγου καὶ σοφίας συγκατατίθεσθαι τοῖς δόγμασιν ἤπερ μετὰ ψιλῆς τῆς πίστεως, καὶ ὅτι κατὰ περίστασιν καὶ τοῦτ᾿ ἐβουλήθη ὁ λόγος, ἵνα μὴ πάντῃ ἀνωφελεῖς ἐάσῃ τοὺς ἀνθρώπους, δηλοῖ ὁ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ γνήσιος μαθητὴς Παῦλος εἰπών· „ἐπειδὴ γὰρ ἐν τῇ σοφίᾳ τοῦ θεοῦ οὐκ ἔγνω ὁ κόσμος διὰ τῆς σοφίας τὸν θεὸν, εὐδόκησεν ὁ θεὸς διὰ τῆς μωρίας τοῦ κηρύγματος σῶσαι τοὺς πιστεύοντας.“ σαφῶς οὖν διὰ τούτων δηλοῦται ὅτι ἐν τῇ σοφίᾳ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐχρῆν γινώσκεσθαι τὸν θεόν. καὶ ἐπεὶ μὴ τοῦτο γεγένηται οὕτως, δεύτερον εὐδόκησεν ὁ θεὸς σῶσαι τοὺς πιστεύοντας οὐχ ἁπαξαπλῶς διὰ μωρίας ἀλλὰ διὰ μωρίας ὅσον ἐπὶ κηρύγματι. αὐτόθεν γὰρ κηρυσσόμενος Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς ἐσταυρωμένος μωρία ἐστὶ κηρύγματος· ὡς καὶ ὁ συναισθόμενος αὐτοῦ λέγει Παῦλος ἐν τῷ· „ἡμεῖς δὲ κηρύσσομεν Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐσταυρωμένον, Ἰουδαίος μὲν σκάνδαλον ἔθνεσι δὲ μωρίαν, αὐτοῖς δὲ τοῖς κλητοῖς, Ἰουδαίοις τε καὶ Ἕλλησι, Χριστὸν θεοῦ δύναμιν καὶ θεοῦ σοφίαν.“
pass_a_gloss: And since Celsus set down as said by many Christians ‘evil indeed is the wisdom in life (ἡ ἐν τῷ βίῳ σοφία), good the foolishness (μωρία)’, it must be said that he slanders (συκοφαντεῖ) the word/teaching (τὸν λόγον), not having set out the very wording (λέξις) lying in Paul, running thus: ‘if anyone thinks (δοκεῖ) to be wise (σοφός) among you, in this age (ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ) let him become foolish (μωρός), that he may become wise; for the wisdom of this world (κόσμος) is foolishness with God (παρὰ θεῷ).’ Therefore the apostle says not simply (ἁπλῶς) ‘the wisdom is foolishness with God’, but ‘the wisdom of this world’; and again not ‘if anyone thinks to be wise among you’ absolutely (ἁπαξαπλῶς) ‘let him become foolish’, but ‘in this age let him become foolish, that he may become wise’. ‘Wisdom’ then ‘of this age’ we call all false-opining (ψευδοδοξοῦσαν) philosophy being abolished (καταργουμένην) according to the Scriptures (γραφαί); and we call foolishness good not absolutely (ἀπολελυμένως), but when someone becomes ‘foolish’ to this age; as if we should say also the Platonist, believing in the immortality (ἀθανασία) of the soul and in the things said about it concerning re-embodiment (μετενσωμάτωσις), has taken up (ἀνειληφέναι) foolishness in relation to the Stoics mocking (διασύροντας) the assent (συγκατάθεσις) of these, and in relation to Peripatetics babbling of Plato’s ‘twitterings’ (τερετίσματα), and in relation to Epicureans charging superstition (δεισιδαιμονία) on those bringing in providence (πρόνοια) and setting God over the wholes (τοῖς ὅλοις). And further, that also according to what pleases the Word/teaching (τὸ τῷ λόγῳ ἀρέσκον) it differs much to assent to doctrines with reason (λόγος) and wisdom than with bare faith (ψιλὴ πίστις), and that by circumstance (κατὰ περίστασιν) the Word willed (ἐβουλήθη) this also, so as not to leave men wholly unhelped (ἀνωφελεῖς), Paul, the genuine (γνήσιος) disciple of Jesus, shows, saying: ‘for since in the wisdom of God the world did not know (οὐκ ἔγνω) God through the wisdom, God was well pleased (εὐδόκησεν) through the foolishness of the preaching (κήρυγμα) to save (σῶσαι) those believing.’ Clearly then through these it is shown that God ought (ἐχρῆν) to be known in the wisdom of God; and since this did not happen thus, secondly (δεύτερον) God was pleased to save the believers, not absolutely through foolishness but through foolishness as far as concerns preaching. For on its face (αὐτόθεν) Jesus Christ crucified (ἐσταυρωμένος), being preached, is foolishness of preaching; as also Paul, perceiving (συναισθόμενος) it, says in the [words]: ‘but we preach Jesus Christ crucified, to Jews a stumbling block (σκάνδαλον), to nations foolishness, but to the called (κλητοί) themselves, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power (δύναμις) of God and the wisdom of God.’
pass_b_english: Celsus has set down, as something said by many Christians, “Wisdom in this life is an evil thing, and foolishness a good one.” We must reply that he slanders our teaching, for he did not set out the actual words found in Paul, which run thus: “If anyone among you thinks he is wise, let him become foolish in this age, so that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Corinthians 3:18–19). So the apostle does not say simply, “Wisdom is foolishness with God,” but “the wisdom of this world”; and again he does not say without qualification, “If anyone among you thinks he is wise, let him become foolish,” but “let him become foolish in this age, so that he may become wise.” By “the wisdom of this age,” then, we mean every philosophy that holds false opinions, which according to the Scriptures is being brought to nothing (1 Corinthians 2:6); and we call foolishness good not absolutely, but when someone becomes “foolish” to this age.

It is as if we were to say that the Platonist too, who believes in the immortality of the soul and in what is said of it concerning its passing into other bodies, has taken up foolishness in the eyes of the Stoics, who mock assent to these things; in the eyes of the Peripatetics, who keep talking of Plato’s “twitterings” (Aristotle, Posterior Analytics 1.22, 83a33); and in the eyes of the Epicureans, who charge with superstition those who bring in providence and set God over the universe.

Further, that even in the judgement of the Word it is far better to assent to doctrines with reason and wisdom than with bare faith, and that the Word willed this also because circumstances required it, so as not to leave human beings wholly without help, is shown by Paul, the true disciple of Jesus, when he says: “For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of the preaching to save those who believe” (1 Corinthians 1:21). These words clearly show that God ought to have been known in the wisdom of God; and since this did not happen so, God was pleased, as a second course, to save those who believe, not through foolishness without qualification, but through foolishness so far as the preaching goes. For Jesus Christ crucified, when he is preached, is at first sight the foolishness of the preaching; as Paul too, who was aware of this, says in the passage: “But we preach Jesus Christ crucified, to Jews a stumbling block and to Gentiles foolishness, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:23–24).

choices.choice: Celsus’s wording here is ‘in this life’ (ἐν τῷ βίῳ), whereas in chapter 9 it was ‘in the world’ (ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ); both are kept as transmitted. In 1 Corinthians 3:18 Origen’s argument joins ‘in this age’ to ‘let him become foolish’, so the quotation is punctuated that way rather than with ‘wise in this age’. ‘Being brought to nothing’ (καταργουμένην) echoes 1 Corinthians 2:6 (where the participle describes the rulers of this age); 1 Corinthians 1:19 (Isaiah 29:14) is also possible. Origen’s text of 1 Corinthians 1:23 reads ‘Jesus Christ’ (Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν), kept. ‘Twitterings’ (τερετίσματα) is Aristotle’s word for the Platonic Forms (Posterior Analytics 1.22, 83a33). ὁ λόγος in ‘the judgement of the Word’ and ‘the Word willed’ can also mean ‘our teaching’; Origen moves between the two senses, and the personal verb ἐβουλήθη favours the Word. ‘This also’ (καὶ τοῦτ᾿) means the way of bare faith. μετενσωμάτωσις rendered ‘passing into other bodies’. ἔθνεσι rendered ‘Gentiles’ in the Pauline quotation.
‘Jesus Christ crucified, preached as he is at first sight’ to ‘Jesus Christ crucified, when he is preached, is at first sight’ so αὐτόθεν qualifies ‘is foolishness’, not the preaching
‘says in the words’ to ‘says in the passage’ (ἐν τῷ), less stiff
